attribution: Ramana Maharshi; his answers to questions put by his early devotee Sivaprakasam Pillai, later arranged in prose
author: ramana-maharshi
period: Answers given around 1901–1902; published in various forms from the 1920s onward
summary: Ramana Maharshi's short classic on self-inquiry: tracing the sense of "I" back to its source.
whyRead: It is perhaps the most direct modern introduction to self-inquiry (atma-vichara). In a few pages it explains what the mind is, where thoughts come from and how to turn attention back to the Self.
story: A young devotee, Sivaprakasam Pillai, put questions to Ramana, who at that time was largely silent and often answered in writing. The answers were later edited into the question-and-answer and essay forms now in print.
questions: What is the mind, and how can it be quietened?
Is liberation something to be gained?

keyTeachings.title: Not the body, not the mind
keyTeachings.text: The text begins by setting aside the body, senses and mind as objects, in the manner of neti neti, pointing to awareness as what remains.

keyTeachings.title: The I-thought
keyTeachings.text: The mind is a bundle of thoughts, and the root of all thoughts is the I-thought. When one inquires into its source, the I-thought subsides.

keyTeachings.title: Self-inquiry as practice
keyTeachings.text: Whenever thoughts arise, one asks to whom they arise and returns attention to the sense of I. Ramana presents this as the most direct method.

keyTeachings.title: Surrender as equivalent
keyTeachings.text: Complete surrender to God is presented as another route to the same end, since both dissolve the ego.

structure.label: Short prose text
structure.note: Circulates in a question-and-answer version and an essay version; the number of questions differs between editions
